1.q: וַ⁠יְהִ֛י בְּ⁠עַשְׁתֵּֽי עֶשְׂרֵ֥ה שָׁנָ֖ה בְּ⁠אֶחָ֣ד לַ⁠חֹ֑דֶשׁ
1.note: Ezekiel is using the phrase translated as **Now it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The implication is that this was **the eleventh year** after King Jehoiachin and Ezekiel had been taken away to Babylon. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the eleventh year after King Jehoiachin and I had been taken into exile, on the first day of the month]
See how you translated this expression in [25:1](ta:25).

2.note: See how you translated **Son of man** in [2:1](ta:02).

2.q: יַ֠עַן אֲשֶׁר אָ֨מְרָה צֹּ֤ר עַל יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙
2.note: Yahweh is speaking of **Tyre** as if it were a living thing that could speak. He means the people of Tyre. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because the people of Tyre have said against Jerusalem]

2.q: אָ֨מְרָה צֹּ֤ר עַל יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ הֶאָ֔ח נִשְׁבְּרָ֛ה דַּלְת֥וֹת הָ⁠עַמִּ֖ים נָסֵ֣בָּה אֵלָ֑⁠י אִמָּלְאָ֖ה הָחֳרָֽבָה
2.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Tyre has said against Jerusalem with delight that the doors of the peoples have been broken, that she has been turned over to Tyre, and that Tyre will be filled now that she has been laid waste]

Tyre is using the word **Aha**, which expresses a strong feeling of malicious delight. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Ha ha]

The expression **The doors of the peoples have been broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that enemies have done the action. Alternate translation: [Enemies have broken the doors of the peoples]

Tyre is speaking as if Jerusalem were **doors** through which **the peoples** passed. Tyre means that Jerusalem controlled the trade of the surrounding nations, and now that Jerusalem has been destroyed, that trade is open to others. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The city that controlled the trade of the peoples has been destroyed]

The pronoun **She** refers to Jerusalem, which Tyre says has now been turned over to it (that is, Tyre controls it). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Jerusalem has been turned over to me]

Here, **turned to me** represents the trade of the nations that used to go through Jerusalem now going to Tyre instead. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Her trade has now come to me]

The expressions **I will be filled** and **she has been laid waste** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that enemies have destroyed Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [I will become full; enemies have laid her waste]

The implication is that Tyre expected to be filled with wealth from the trade that used to go through Jerusalem. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will be filled with wealth from her trade]

3.q: לָ⁠כֵ֗ן כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֔ה הִנְ⁠נִ֥י עָלַ֖יִ⁠ךְ צֹ֑ר
3.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [therefore I, the Lord Yahweh, declare that I am against you, Tyre]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4. This also occurs in verses 7, 15, and 19.

The point of this comparison is that just as **the sea brings up its waves** one after another against the shore, so Yahweh will bring up **many nations** to attack Tyre one after another. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [who will come against you one after another without end]

4.q: וְ⁠שִׁחֲת֞וּ חֹמ֣וֹת צֹ֗ר וְ⁠הָֽרְסוּ֙ מִגְדָּלֶ֔י⁠הָ וְ⁠סִֽחֵיתִ֥י עֲפָרָ֖⁠הּ מִמֶּ֑⁠נָּה וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֥י אוֹתָ֖⁠הּ לִ⁠צְחִ֥יחַ סָֽלַע
4.note: Even though Yahweh is addressing Tyre directly, he is speaking of it in the third person as **Tyre** and **her**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [And they will destroy your walls, Tyre, and tear down your towers. And I will scrape your dust from you, and I will make you as a bare surface of a rock. ]

4.q: וְ⁠סִֽחֵיתִ֥י עֲפָרָ֖⁠הּ מִמֶּ֑⁠נָּה וְ⁠נָתַתִּ֥י אוֹתָ֖⁠הּ לִ⁠צְחִ֥יחַ סָֽלַע
4.note: Yahweh is speaking as if Tyre were a piece of ground whose soil he would **scrape** away until only **a bare surface of a rock** remained. He means that he will destroy the city so completely that nothing will be left of it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will destroy her so completely that nothing of her will be left]

5.note: This could mean: (1) the city’s location will become a place useless for anything but drying fishing nets. Alternate translation: [She will become a place to dry nets, surrounded by the sea] (2) the sea will cover over where the city used to be and people will fish in that location. Alternate translation: [The place where the city was will be under the sea and people will fish there]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:11. This also occurs in verses 14 and 21.

6.note: The expression **will be killed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that enemy soldiers will do the action. Alternate translation: [And enemy soldiers will kill her daughters who are in the field with the sword]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the towns and villages that depended on Tyre were **her daughters**. The phrase **who are in the field** indicates that these towns were on the mainland, not on the island where Tyre was. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people in the mainland towns that depend on her]
Here, **the sword** represents “warfare.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in warfare]
See how you translated the similar expression in 6:7.

7.note: The implication is that Nebuchadnezzar and his army would come **from the north** because armies from Babylon traveled around the desert and entered the region from the north, even though Babylon itself was to the east. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from the north, traveling around the desert from Babylon in the east]

The phrase **a king of kings** is a title. The implication is that Nebuchadnezzar was the greatest of kings, who ruled over many other kings. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a king who rules over many other kings]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **horse** or **chariot**. He means horses and chariots in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with horses and with chariots and with horsemen]

The implication is that **an assembly and a great people** refers to a large army of soldiers. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and a large assembly of soldiers, a great army]

8.q: וְ⁠נָתַ֨ן עָלַ֜יִ⁠ךְ דָּיֵ֗ק וְ⁠שָׁפַ֤ךְ עָלַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ סֹֽלְלָ֔ה וְ⁠הֵקִ֥ים עָלַ֖יִ⁠ךְ צִנָּֽה
8.note: A **siege wall** is a kind of wall that an army built around a city to keep people from going in or out. A **siege mound** is a kind of ramp of earth that an army piled up against a city wall so that soldiers could climb over it. A **large shield** is a kind of shield that soldiers set up to protect themselves while they attacked a city. If your readers would not be familiar with these things, you could use the names of similar things that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. Alternate translation: [And he will build a wall around you to trap you, and he will pile up a ramp of dirt against your walls, and he will set up big shields to protect his soldiers as they attack you]

9.note: A **battering ram** is a kind of heavy beam that soldiers pounded against a wall or gate to break it down. If your readers would not be familiar with what a battering ram is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [And the blow of his heavy wall-smashing log]

Here, **swords** represents “weapons and tools made of iron.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and your towers he will break down with his iron weapons and tools]

10.note: Yahweh says **their dust will cover you** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that Nebuchadnezzar will have so many horses that the dust they stir up will seem to cover the whole city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [From the abundance of his horses a great cloud of dust will rise over you]

The point of this comparison is that just as soldiers easily enter **a city broken open** through the gaps in its walls, so Nebuchadnezzar will easily ride **into your gates**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as easily as soldiers enter a city whose walls have been broken down]

11.note: The implication is that **the pillars of your strength** are the sacred stone pillars that the people of Tyre had set up for their gods and in which they took great pride. Alternatively, the phrase may refer to the strong fortifications of the city. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the sacred stone pillars for your gods in which you take pride will fall to the ground]

12.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar’s army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar will spoil your wealth and plunder your merchandise]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **houses** that are characterized by **desire**, that is, houses that the people of Tyre considered beautiful and valuable. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and break down your desirable houses]

13.q: וְ⁠הִשְׁבַּתִּ֖י הֲמ֣וֹן שִׁירָ֑יִ⁠ךְ וְ⁠ק֣וֹל כִּנּוֹרַ֔יִ⁠ךְ לֹ֥א יִשָּׁמַ֖ע עֽוֹד
13.note: Here, **the multitude of your songs** and **the sound of your harps** represent “the joyful celebrations” of the people of Tyre. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And I will make all your joyful singing celebrations cease, and your festive music will not be heard again]

The expression **will not be heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that no one will hear the sound. Alternate translation: [and no one will hear the sound of your harps again]

14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a bare surface of a rock** is flat and barren, with nothing growing or built on it, so Tyre will become. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I will make you like a flat, bare rock]

Yahweh is speaking of Tyre as if it would become a **spreading place of nets**, a place where fishermen spread their nets out to dry. He means that Tyre will be reduced to a deserted shore where fishermen come to work rather than a great city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will become nothing but a place where fishermen dry their nets]

The expression **You will not be built again** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one will build you again]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:15.

15.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֣א מִ⁠קּ֣וֹל מַפַּלְתֵּ֗⁠ךְ בֶּ⁠אֱנֹ֨ק חָלָ֜ל בֵּ⁠הָ֤רֵֽג הֶ֨רֶג֙ בְּ⁠תוֹכֵ֔⁠ךְ יִרְעֲשׁ֖וּ הָ⁠אִיִּֽים
15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that **the coastlands** will certainly **shake** when Tyre falls. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The coastlands will certainly shake from the sound of your fall, when the slain one groans, when slaughter is slaughtered in your midst!]

Here, **the coastlands** represents “the people who live along the coasts.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people living by the sea]

The expression **slaughter is slaughtered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when enemy soldiers kill many people in your midst]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

16.note: Here, **the sea** represents “the nations along the coasts of the sea.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of the princes of the coastal nations]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **garments** that are characterized by **embroidery**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [their embroidered garments]

16.q: וְ⁠הֵסִ֨ירוּ֙ אֶת מְעִ֣ילֵי⁠הֶ֔ם וְ⁠אֶת בִּגְדֵ֥י רִקְמָתָ֖⁠ם יִפְשֹׁ֑טוּ & עַל הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ יֵשֵׁ֔בוּ
16.note: Removing their robes and fine clothing and sitting on the ground were symbolic actions by which the princes showed that they were mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **tremblings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [They will begin to shake fearfully]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if **tremblings** were clothing that the princes would **put on** in place of the robes they had removed. He means that they will be very afraid and tremble. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will be very afraid and tremble]

Yahweh is using **at moments** as a common expression of the culture to mean “continually.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will tremble continually]

Yahweh is using **be desolate over you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be horrified at what has happened to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will be appalled at what has happened to you]

17.note: Ezekiel is speaking as if a lamentation were an object that people could **take up**. It means that they will begin to sing a mournful song about Tyre. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they will raise a lamentation over you] or [And they will sing a lamentation over you]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it from here through the end of the next verse.

The princes are using the phrase **How you have perished** to express a strong feeling of grief. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas, you have been utterly destroyed]

The implication could be 1) that Tyre was a city **inhabited** by people who came **from the seas**, that is, seafaring people who traded by ship. Alternate translation: [O city inhabited by seafaring traders] or 2) that Tyre was a city where people lived even though it was out in the sea on an island. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [O city surrounded by the sea]

The expression **praised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that many people praised the city. Alternate translation: [the city that many people praised]

17.q: אֲשֶׁר֩ הָיְתָ֨ה חֲזָקָ֤ה בַ⁠יָּם֙ הִ֣יא וְ⁠יֹשְׁבֶ֔י⁠הָ
17.note: Even though the princes are addressing Tyre directly, they are speaking of it in the third person as **she** and **her**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [you who were strong in the sea, you and your inhabitants]

The sea princes are speaking of **terror** as if it were an object that could be placed on people. They mean that Tyre caused all her inhabitants to feel terror. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who caused all her inhabitants to feel terror] or [who terrified all of her inhabitants]

The pronoun **her** refers to the region around Tyre, so **her inhabitants** are the people who lived along the coasts. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on all of the people who lived along her coasts]

18.q: עַתָּה֙ יֶחְרְד֣וּ הָֽ⁠אִיִּ֔ן י֖וֹם מַפַּלְתֵּ֑⁠ךְ וְ⁠נִבְהֲל֛וּ הָ⁠אִיִּ֥ים אֲשֶׁר בַּ⁠יָּ֖ם מִ⁠צֵּאתֵֽ⁠ךְ
18.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Now all the coastlands in the sea will shake with great terror on the day of your fall]

The expression **will be terrified** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that the fall of Tyre will terrify them. Alternate translation: [and the coastlands that are in the sea will shake with fear]

Here the princes of the sea are speaking of Tyre’s destruction as if it were Tyre **going out**, as a person leaves a place and does not return. It means that Tyre will cease to exist. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by your light going out] or [by your destruction]

19.q: עִ֣יר נֶחֱרֶ֔בֶת כֶּ⁠עָרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא נוֹשָׁ֑בוּ
19.note: The expressions **laid waste** and **have not been inhabited** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that Yahweh will destroy the city and that no one lives in those other cities. Alternate translation: [a city that I have destroyed, like the cities where no one has lived]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the cities that have not been inhabited** are empty ruins, so Tyre will be empty and in ruins. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [empty and in ruins like the cities that have not been inhabited]

19.q: בְּ⁠הַעֲל֤וֹת עָלַ֨יִ⁠ךְ֙ אֶת תְּה֔וֹם וְ⁠כִסּ֖וּ⁠ךְ הַ⁠מַּ֥יִם הָ⁠רַבִּֽים
19.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the destruction of Tyre were **the deep** sea rising up and **the many waters** covering the city. He means that he will completely overwhelm Tyre with disaster. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I overwhelm you completely with disaster and destroy you entirely]

20.note: Yahweh is using **bring you down with the ones going down to the pit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy you so that you join those who have died and been buried.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then I will kill you so that you go to the place of the dead]

Yahweh is using **a people of eternity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people who died long ago.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the people who died in ancient times]

Yahweh is speaking as if the place of the dead were **the land of the lower parts**, a land far beneath the earth. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the place of the dead]

The phrase **And I will put splendor in the land of the living** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [And you will not stand in the land of the living]

21.note: Here, **terrors** represents “a terrifying disaster.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will bring a terrifying disaster on you]

The expressions **you will be sought** and **you will not be found** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you do so, you could say that people will search for Tyre but will never find it. Alternate translation: [And people will look for you, but no one will find you again forever]
